idiom_name: header struct + length-prefixed payload frame (wire format by hand); POSIX mq_send byte message
implementation_notes: The C standard library has no message type, so the package is built by hand: one struct holds the header fields (type tag, flags, correlation id, body length) and the payload follows as a byte buffer, serialized field by field with fixed-width types and a defined byte order. On POSIX systems the OS can carry the package itself - mq_open/mq_send/mq_receive move an opaque byte message with a priority (msg_prio) through a named queue bounded by mq_maxmsg and mq_msgsize per message - but the header/body split inside that byte message is still yours to define, serialize and validate. The hand-written struct form remains justified whenever the wire format is fixed by an external protocol or allocation must be avoided.
pitfalls: Struct padding and endianness make the in-memory header differ from the wire header; serialize field by field (or fix the layout) instead of memcpy-ing the struct.
A body length taken from the header without validation is a buffer-overflow vector: bound it against the frame size (or mq_msgsize) before allocating or reading.

POSIX queues bound both message size and queue depth (mq_msgsize, mq_maxmsg) and fail with EAGAIN/EMSGSIZE when full or oversized; stream sockets require a framing convention because read() can return partial headers.
